dof-simulator.beginner: Depth of field is the zone of your photo — from near to far — that looks acceptably sharp. Three controls shape that zone: aperture (wider apertures blur the background more), focal length (longer lenses narrow the zone), and subject distance (moving closer shrinks it further). Adjust any of them here and watch the depth ruler and viewport update together in real time.

0.heading: Aperture Geometry and the Circle of Confusion
0.text: A lens focuses light from one exact distance onto the sensor as a perfect point; everything else lands as a small disc called the circle of confusion (CoC). A point still reads as sharp as long as its disc stays smaller than a threshold set by sensor size — roughly 0.03mm on full frame. Widening the aperture (lowering the f-number) opens a larger cone of light between the lens and the point of focus, so points away from that plane spread into much larger discs, much faster. That's why a wide aperture like f/1.4 blurs the background so much more than f/11 — it's the geometry of the light cone changing, not just the amount of light.

1.heading: Focal Length and Distance Dominate the Effect
1.text: Focal length's effect on depth of field depends entirely on what you hold constant. At a fixed subject distance, depth of field narrows sharply with focal length — roughly with its square: standing 3m from a subject at f/2.8, a 35mm lens gives about 1.3m of depth of field, while a 200mm lens gives about 35mm. But that comparison also changes your framing, since you didn't reframe. At a fixed framing — this tool's lock-FOV mode, where you walk back as you zoom in to keep the subject the same size — depth of field barely moves: sweeping 35mm to 200mm at f/2.8 with framing locked changes total depth of field by well under 1%. What changes dramatically instead is the background: a longer lens magnifies and compresses everything behind your subject, so out-of-focus highlights grow larger and the background separates more, even though the in-focus slab around your subject stays about the same thickness. Turn on lock-FOV and sweep focal length to watch it happen — the depth-of-field readout holds steady while the background blur figure climbs. Subject distance remains the more reliable lever either way: moving closer at a fixed focal length and aperture shrinks depth of field sharply, pulling the near and far limits tighter around a shorter distance.

2.heading: Sensor Size and Equivalent Framing
2.text: To fill the frame with the same subject, a larger sensor needs a proportionally longer focal length than a smaller one — a full-frame camera needs roughly 1.5x the focal length of an APS-C camera, and about 2x that of Micro Four Thirds, for the same field of view. Because depth of field narrows with focal length, that longer 'equivalent' focal length is what gives full-frame cameras their reputation for shallower depth of field — the f-number printed on the lens doesn't tell the whole story. Two lenses at the same f-stop on different sensor sizes, framed identically, will produce meaningfully different depth of field.

0.label: Aperture
0.description: Wider apertures (low f-numbers like f/1.4-f/2.8) open a steeper light cone and shrink depth of field. Narrower apertures (f/8-f/16) widen it.

1.label: Focal Length
1.description: At a fixed subject distance, depth of field narrows roughly with the square of focal length. At a fixed framing (zoom in and step back to keep the same shot), depth of field barely changes — it's the background that transforms, growing more magnified and blurred as focal length increases.

2.label: Subject Distance
2.description: Moving closer to your subject shrinks depth of field faster than almost any other adjustment, which is why macro photography has such razor-thin sharp zones.

3.label: Sensor Size
3.description: Larger sensors need longer focal lengths to match the same framing as smaller sensors, which indirectly produces shallower depth of field at equivalent shots.

0.text: At wide apertures like f/1.4-f/2.0, depth of field can be thinner than a human face. Focus precisely on the near eye, not the nose or ear, or your subject's gaze will read as soft.

1.text: Use the framing presets (Face, Portrait, Medium Shot, and so on) to lock your subject's size in the frame while you experiment — they hold focal length and distance in the same relationship a real shot would, so the blur you see here matches what you'd get in camera.

2.text: Don't chase maximum depth of field by stopping all the way down — most lenses are sharpest around f/8-f/11, well before this tool's diffraction warning appears. That warning is a stricter, later threshold: it only lights up once diffraction blur exceeds the sensor's circle of confusion, which happens around f/22 on full frame (f/15 on APS-C, f/11 on Micro Four Thirds). Treat f/8-f/11 as your practical target, and the warning chip as the outer limit, not the goal.

focalLength.definition: The distance in millimeters from the optical center of the lens to the sensor when focused at infinity. Longer focal lengths magnify the image and narrow the depth of field.

aperture.definition: The size of the lens opening, expressed as an f-number (e.g., f/2.8). Lower f-numbers mean a wider opening, letting in more light and producing a shallower depth of field.

subjectDistance.definition: The distance from the camera to the point of focus. Closer focus distances result in a shallower depth of field.

sensor.definition: The physical dimensions of the camera sensor. Larger sensors (full-frame, medium format) require longer focal lengths for equivalent framing, which produces shallower depth of field than smaller sensors (APS-C, Micro Four Thirds).

hyperfocal.definition: The focus distance that maximizes depth of field. When you focus at this distance, everything from half the hyperfocal distance to infinity appears sharp.

coc.definition: The maximum diameter of a blur spot on the sensor that still appears as a point to the human eye. Determines the boundary of acceptable sharpness for depth-of-field calculations.

backgroundBlur.definition: A measure of how blurred the background appears behind your subject. Higher values mean stronger blur and more subject isolation.

diffractionWarning.definition: At very small apertures, light bends around the aperture edges, softening the image. This tool's diffraction warning appears once that softening exceeds the sensor's circle of confusion — around f/22 on full frame, f/15 on APS-C, f/11 on Micro Four Thirds.

0.scenario: You're photographing a portrait and want the background to melt into a soft blur behind your subject. Which aperture should you choose?
0.hint: Lower f-numbers mean a wider opening — and a shallower depth of field.
0.successMessage: Right — f/1.4 opens the aperture wide, producing a shallow depth of field and a smoothly blurred background.
0.failureMessage: Not quite. Higher f-numbers like f/11 or f/16 keep more of the scene sharp. For maximum background blur, pick the widest aperture (the lowest f-number) instead.

1.scenario: You're photographing four friends arranged in a loose cluster — a couple of them are a half-step forward or back from the others. Which aperture gives you a comfortable safety margin to keep everyone sharp?
1.hint: You need extra depth of field to cover people who aren't in the exact same focal plane, but you don't need to stop all the way down.
1.successMessage: Correct — f/5.6 provides a comfortable buffer of depth of field for small variations in distance, without narrowing the aperture more than necessary.
1.failureMessage: f/1.4 is too shallow for people at slightly different distances, and f/16 stops down further than you need. f/5.6 is the reliable middle ground.

2.scenario: You're at 85mm, f/1.8, with your subject 3 meters away, and you want to noticeably increase background blur without touching the aperture or switching lenses. What's the fastest way?
2.hint: Depth of field — and how strongly the background blurs relative to your subject — is extremely sensitive to subject distance.
2.successMessage: Exactly — halving the subject distance dramatically shrinks depth of field and magnifies background blur, without changing your aperture or lens.
2.failureMessage: Moving farther away or raising ISO won't shrink depth of field. Getting closer to your subject is the fastest way to increase background blur at a fixed aperture and focal length.

0.label: Move to 1.5m from your subject (half the distance)

1.label: Move to 6m from your subject (double the distance)

2.label: Step back to increase your working distance

3.label: Raise the ISO for a brighter background

3.scenario: You're shooting a landscape on a full-frame camera and want maximum sharpness across the whole frame. Should you stop all the way down to f/22 for the most depth of field?
3.hint: There's a trade-off between the depth of field gained by stopping down and the softening caused by diffraction at very small apertures.
3.successMessage: Right — f/22 does add depth of field on paper, but most lenses are already past their sharpest apertures by then. A moderate aperture like f/8-f/11 usually balances depth of field and lens sharpness better. This tool's own diffraction warning is a separate, later threshold — it flags only once diffraction blur exceeds the sensor's circle of confusion, which on full frame doesn't happen until around f/22 (f/15 on APS-C, f/11 on Micro Four Thirds). Don't wait for that warning before backing off — it's a hard physical limit, not a sharpness recommendation.
3.failureMessage: Stopping all the way down to f/22 does maximize depth of field on paper, but most lenses have already passed their sharpest aperture range by then. A moderate aperture like f/8-f/11 usually gives a better balance of depth of field and real-world sharpness. This tool's diffraction warning is a separate, later threshold — it only appears once blur exceeds the sensor's circle of confusion, around f/22 on full frame — so don't use its absence as a green light to keep stopping down.

0.label: Yes — always use the smallest aperture available for maximum depth of field

1.label: No — use a moderate aperture like f/8-f/11 for the best overall sharpness, not the smallest one

2.label: No — use the widest aperture available for the sharpest results

3.label: It doesn't matter — aperture has no effect on sharpness

4.scenario: You're comparing two setups for the same portrait framing: a full-frame camera with an 85mm f/1.8 lens, and an APS-C camera (1.5x crop) with a 56mm f/1.8 lens producing the same field of view. Which produces shallower depth of field?
4.hint: Compare the actual (not equivalent) focal length each lens uses to achieve the same framing.
4.successMessage: Correct — even though both lenses are f/1.8, the full-frame camera uses a longer actual focal length (85mm vs. 56mm) to match the framing, which produces noticeably shallower depth of field.
4.failureMessage: Both lenses share the same f-number, but the full-frame camera needs a longer actual focal length to match the framing. That longer focal length is what produces shallower depth of field — not the f-number alone.

2.label: Both produce identical depth of field
